newsitem.title: USA: NYS Pataki sees state roaring ahead, critics don't.
newsitem.headline: NYS Pataki sees state roaring ahead, critics don't.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki on Wednesday said his program of big tax cuts, job growth and more money for schools and the environment was sending the state roaring into the next century.

But critics were swift to deride Pataki's promises, saying he had failed to create new jobs, forced local communities to raise taxes, and was pushing for too many harsh changes in a new welfare bill needed to comply with the federal changes. The governor has estimated that his Administration's efforts already have trimmed welfare rolls by around 220,000.

In his State of the State address, the governor promised that when they looked back, voters would see "that these were the years when New Yorkers roared into the 21st century, ready to fulfill their destiny."

The governor's speech, which focused on bread-and-butter issues, like using $1.75 billion of new bond act dollars to clean-up the state's air, water and land, helping ensure that every school has computers by the end of the century, and new measures to combat domestic violence and give the police more crime-fighting powers, offered few details about the 1998 fiscal budget that he will propose next week, though he said schools would get an additional $250 million of aid.

Pataki, whose large income tax cuts have been criticized by civic and local groups for shifting the burden to cities and towns forcing them to raise property taxes, vowed to cut property taxes by hundreds of millions of dollars with a new, multi-year program.

He promised New Yorkers that they would again see their taxes fall more than the residents of any other state, estimating that by the end of 1997, the third year of his income tax reductions, New York familes will have saved $6.5 billion that they previously paid the state.

Citing examples of companies that are expanding, like Fidelity Investment, which is hiring more than 600 workers at a World Trade Center office in New York City, Pataki told New Yorkers his tax cuts would produce more jobs.
"We've only begun to create new jobs because we've only begun to cut taxes. We must do more," Pataki told lawmakers.

However, State Comptroller H. Carl McCall, a Democrat, attacked the governor's policies, calling his job growth strategy "a bust," as it ranks near the bottom of all states, and noting that while New York ranked 26th in state taxes, it is the nation's leader, by a big margin, in local taxes.
"But I'm most concerned about what's not in the message from the governor. He still has not developed a comprehensive strategy for creating jobs," McCall said in a prepared statement.
The fiscal monitor also faulted the governor for failing to address "overwhelming financial difficulties" faced by cities throughout the state, like Yonkers, Newburgh, Troy, Utica and Buffalo.
State Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, (R-Troy), who also has proposed property tax relief, vowed to work with Pataki to enact tax cuts to make the state more competitive.

He added the Senate wanted to focus on creating private sector jobs for welfare participants shifted to workfare programs, but was willing to study Pataki's proposal to have them help renovate state properties as a transitional measure.

Other groups blasted the governor's new welfare plan, which imposes strict new work requirements, with one nonprofit, advocacy group, Housing Works, saying 17 of its AIDS activists, who had chained themselves together outside the Assembly Chamber just before the governor spoke, were arrested, according to a prepared statement.

The Coalition for the Homeless, another advocacy group, called Pataki's new welfare bill "cruel," estimating that it would double the number of rate of homeless people on welfare, causing New York City's homeless population to leap 100,000.

Increasing the shelter allowence to cover the real cost of rent or using an equivalent rent subsidy would eliminate nine out of 10 episodes of homelessness in the state, and save it as well as local districts and the federal government over $500 million a year, the group added in prepared remarks.
